entities.name: Gregory Tifernas
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Gregory Tifernas (died 1464) was a pivotal Italian Renaissance humanist and prolific translator, whose profound mastery of Greek and Latin facilitated the transmission of classical Hellenic thought into Quattrocento Italy. Born in Città di Castello, Umbria, to a family of Greek origin, Tifernas played a crucial role in the intellectual revival of the 15th century by making previously inaccessible Greek texts available to Western scholars. His work directly contributed to the burgeoning Neoplatonism and Aristotelian scholarship that defined the Florentine and Roman academies, thereby influencing figures like Lorenzo de' Medici and Pope Nicholas V.

Tifernas's career was marked by extensive translation efforts and academic appointments across Italy. He served as a professor of Greek in Venice, Florence, and Rome, where he taught a new generation of humanists the subtleties of classical Greek. Among his most significant achievements were the Latin translations of Aristotle's *Poetics* (c. 1450) and *Rhetoric*, which had a transformative impact on literary theory and oratorical practice. He also translated works by Xenophon, Plato, and Demosthenes, directly shaping the curriculum and intellectual discourse of the early Renaissance. His meticulous approach to translation, emphasizing fidelity to the original Greek, set new scholarly standards.

The translations produced by Gregory Tifernas became fundamental resources for Western European scholarship, circulating widely in manuscript form and later through early printed editions. His efforts not only expanded the corpus of classical texts available in the West but also deepened the understanding of Greek philosophy and rhetoric, underpinning the intellectual foundations of the High Renaissance. The availability of these texts spurred new critical engagement with classical thought, influencing fields from aesthetics to political theory and shaping the educational paradigm for centuries.

His efforts directly facilitated the widespread study of classical Greek thought across Italy and beyond, profoundly influencing subsequent generations of scholars and artists.
